Hi! My name is Ahmad. I’m a high school student specializing in web development—I build web applications using React and work with Git/GitHub. I’m interested in space, AI, web development, server-side operations.

We are participating in a local event in Dushanbe. Our goal is to create a functional tool for future astronaut missions to Mars, complete with features like route planning and the visualization of various types of location data. We also aim to deliver good presentation of our project.
summary:
SpaceMap is an interactive platform for planning exploration of the Martian surface, based on NASA data.

What the project does:
• Integrates optical, thermal, spectral, topographical, and atmospheric data into an interface featuring both a 2D map and a 3D globe.
• Displays mission landing sites and archival NASA panoramas, allowing users to familiarize themselves with the terrain in advance.
• Enables users to set target coordinates, compare direct routes with alternatives that account for terrain slopes, and plan multi-stop expeditions.
• Provides local weather observations, estimated lighting conditions, and projected travel durations.

How it supports astronauts:
It assists in selecting sites for geological research and sample collection, analyzing terrain prior to extravehicular activity (EVA), determining the sequence of scientific stops, and planning the return journey. Data on the terrain and environmental conditions help identify, in advance, specific issues that may require further investigation.

Why it matters:
SpaceMap consolidates disparate NASA datasets into a single workspace, linking scientific objectives directly to expedition planning. It serves as a decision-support prototype: while it helps in preparing a route, it does not guarantee safety—local obstacles, radiation levels, and crew resource constraints must still be verified.
details:
SpaceMap - A Platform for Planning Mars Exploration

SpaceMap integrates NASA data into an interactive interface designed to assist in the preparation of scientific expeditions: selecting research areas, studying the surface, mapping out routes, and estimating travel time. The intended use case is a mission-planning workstation located within the habitat module of a Mars mission.

Scientific Objectives

The platform helps astronauts select sites for geological observation and sample collection. For instance, a team might begin by focusing on the Gale Crater and Mount Sharp region, using findings from the Curiosity rover as a foundation for developing their own research program. By cross-referencing imagery, terrain features, and mineralogical data, users can identify which areas warrant more detailed investigation.

Maps and NASA Data

The project features both a 2D map and a 3D globe, with the ability to toggle between various thematic layers:

Optical imagery: for surface reconnaissance and examining local details.

Thermal data: for comparing the thermal properties of different locations.

Spectral and mineralogical data: for identifying variations in surface composition.

MOLA topography: for assessing elevation and major landforms.

Atmospheric data: including historical dust maps and local weather observations.

The platform draws primarily from NASA Mars Trek, the NASA Image and Video Library, and data from various Mars missions. As the user zooms in, the map automatically loads higher-resolution imagery where available; coverage and resolution vary depending on the selected dataset.

Exploring Research Sites

Mission-specific markers provide access to archived NASA panoramas, allowing users to familiarize themselves with the terrain and landmarks in a given area before arrival. Each entry includes the date the image was captured and a link to the original source. These panoramas represent historical observations rather than the current conditions at any given location on Mars.

Routes and Expeditions

Users can define their starting coordinates and target destinations. The planner compares a direct path with an alternative route that accounts for slope constraints based on MOLA elevation data. This helps identify major terrain features that could impede movement.

For more complex expeditions, users can select multiple waypoints, include a return leg, specify a departure date, choose a mode of transport, and define the duration of exploration at each location. Based on these inputs, the project generates a tentative schedule measured in Martian days-sols.

Crew Operational Conditions

SpaceMap displays available observations from the Curiosity rover’s REMS instrument, including the date and distance from the selected area. Additionally, the system calculates lighting conditions and various environmental parameters using predictive models. This facilitates discussions regarding the timing of extravehicular activities (EVAs) and the sequence of tasks, while clearly distinguishing between actual recorded measurements and calculated estimates.

S.A.M. Assistant

The project integrates Gemini via a Python server. The assistant accesses the context of the selected map and is designed to provide explanations regarding data layers, mission objectives, and routes. The API key is stored securely on the server. The stability of the Gemini connection is still subject to further testing.

Technical Implementation

The interface is built using JavaScript with Three.js for visualization. Vite is used for client-side bundling, while Python and FastAPI handle the website and API. A Docker container has been prepared for deployment.

Significance and Limitations

SpaceMap links scientific objectives to specific exploration plans, reducing the need to consult multiple disparate data sources. However, the project remains a decision-support prototype. Actual astronaut EVAs would require rigorous verification of local terrain obstacles and soil conditions, radiation levels, oxygen and energy reserves, and emergency return protocols. A route calculated based on regional topography alone cannot be considered definitively safe.
